questions.prompt: Why does this course say hands-on practice matters more for Salesforce than for many other IT skills?
options: Because Salesforce is almost entirely point-and-click configuration, and certification exams are scenario-based, so recognizing which Setup page solves a problem only comes from repetition.
Because Salesforce certification exams only accept answers typed directly into a live org during the test.
Because reading Salesforce documentation is forbidden by Salesforce's terms of service.
Because Setup pages change their layout every single day, so memorizing them from reading is impossible.
questions.explain: Salesforce administration happens almost entirely in Setup, a clicks-first configuration tool, and certification exams describe business scenarios rather than asking for definitions. Recognizing which Setup page solves a given problem only comes from having actually clicked through Setup repeatedly, not from reading about it.

questions.prompt: Per this course, which of these is a real mistake to avoid when creating your Trailhead account?
options: Signing up using a Salesforce trial org's login, since trial orgs expire on a fixed schedule and can't be reactivated.
Signing up using a Salesforce trial org's login, since trial orgs require a credit card that gets charged automatically after 30 days.
Signing up with Slack, since Slack logins can't be linked to a Trailhead Playground.
Setting your Trailblazer Profile Privacy to Public, since Public profiles are deleted automatically after 90 days of inactivity.
Using an email address you'll still have access to in a year, since Trailhead charges a renewal fee to that email annually.
Choosing a username that doesn't use your full legal name, since Trailhead requires a verified legal name within 30 days.
questions.explain: This course warns against signing up with a Salesforce trial org's login specifically because trial orgs expire on a fixed schedule and can't be reactivated — if that login expires, the Trailhead account tied to it, including all its badges and trails, becomes inaccessible.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B also centers on the trial-org mistake, but gets the actual reason wrong. Trailhead's sign-up flow never asks for payment at all — there's no credit card to be charged. The real problem is that trial orgs expire on a fixed schedule and can't be reactivated, which is what actually costs you access to the tied Trailhead account.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Trailhead Playground is, underneath the friendly name, a real ________ org.
questions.explain: Every Trailhead Playground's Company Information page reads 'Developer Edition' under Organization Edition — the friendly 'Playground' name is just Trailhead's label on top of a genuine Developer Edition org.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Developer Edition orgs, per this course.
options: A Developer Edition org doesn't expire on a fixed countdown, unlike a 30-day trial org.
A Developer Edition org is capped at two paid user licenses and roughly 10MB of data storage.
A Developer Edition org supports installing packages from the AppExchange, the same as a paid org.
A Developer Edition org has a stripped-down Setup with several admin features disabled.
A Developer Edition org requires a credit card on file before it can be provisioned.
questions.explain: Developer Edition doesn't expire like a trial, and it's capped (two paid user licenses, ~10MB storage) rather than crippled — the full admin feature set, including AppExchange package installation, works exactly as it would in a paid org. No credit card is required to provision one.

questions.prompt: A new admin says, 'I'll just create a sandbox to practice in, before I've even gotten a job.' Per this course, why doesn't that plan work?
options: A sandbox only exists in relation to a specific company's paid production org, and only someone with admin access to that production org can create one — there's no company org to copy from yet.
Sandboxes are more expensive than Developer Edition orgs, so Salesforce blocks personal use entirely.
A sandbox requires exactly the same Trailhead account used to create a Trailhead Playground, so one org must be deleted first.
Sandboxes can only be created by Salesforce support staff, never by any admin, under any circumstances.
questions.explain: A sandbox is always a copy of one specific, real production org, belonging to whichever company owns that org. Without a company's paid production org to copy, and without admin access to it, there's nothing to create a sandbox from — unlike a Trailhead Playground, which starts empty and belongs to you personally.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 environment term to what it actually is.
right: A copy of a specific company's real, paid production org
A free Developer Edition org, created and managed through Trailhead
The same free org type, signed up for directly outside Trailhead
questions.explain: A Trailhead Playground is a free Developer Edition org created through Trailhead. A standalone Developer Edition org is the exact same org type, signed up for directly at developer.salesforce.com. A sandbox is fundamentally different — a copy of one specific company's real, paid production org.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating and starting to use a Trailhead Playground, per this course, in the correct order.
items: Sign up for a free Trailhead account
Open a hands-on challenge or the Hands-On Orgs page and click Create Playground
Name the new org something recognizable
Wait a few minutes while Salesforce provisions the org
Launch into Setup from the Hands-On Orgs page
questions.explain: Chapter 1 walks this exact sequence: create a Trailhead account first, then start the Create Playground flow, name the org something recognizable, wait for provisioning (typically three to four minutes), and finally launch into the finished org's Setup.

questions.prompt: A new admin clicks the grid icon in the Salesforce header, expecting to reach Setup, but lands somewhere else entirely. Per this course, what actually happened, and what should they click instead?
options: The grid icon opens the App Launcher, for switching apps and records — Setup is the separate gear icon next to it.
The grid icon opens Setup exactly as expected, and the admin simply hasn't finished loading the page yet.
The grid icon opens the App Launcher, which is actually the same screen as Setup under a different name — no separate gear icon exists.
The grid icon opens Quick Find, a search box scoped only to Object Manager.
The grid icon opens the Trailblazer Community directory, not any Salesforce configuration screen.
The grid icon opens the admin's personal Settings page, reached otherwise only from the profile photo.
questions.explain: The grid icon opens the App Launcher, for switching between installed apps and jumping to records. Setup is opened from the separate gear icon sitting right next to it — a common early mix-up precisely because the two icons sit so close together in the header.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C also correctly names the App Launcher, but gets the one detail wrong that matters: the App Launcher and Setup are not the same screen. They sit right next to each other in the header as two distinct icons — gear for Setup, grid for the App Launcher — and confusing the two is exactly the mix-up this lesson calls out.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Quick Find and Search Setup, per this course.
options: Search Setup searches every Setup page in the org by name, regardless of where you currently are.
The sidebar's Quick Find filters whatever category list is currently in view.
Object Manager has its own Quick Find, scoped to the list currently open on that object's page.
Quick Find and Search Setup are two names for the exact same single search box.
The App Launcher's search box works on a completely different mechanism than Quick Find.
questions.explain: Search Setup searches every Setup page by name regardless of location, the sidebar's Quick Find filters the currently-viewed category list, and Object Manager has its own scoped Quick Find. These are genuinely different boxes, not the same one by two names — and the App Launcher's search box works on the identical live-filter pattern, not a different mechanism.

questions.prompt: A teammate is locked out of their Salesforce login. Per this course, who should perform the reset, and from where?
options: An admin, from Setup → Users → Reset Password(s), since resetting someone else's password requires admin permissions an ordinary user doesn't have.
The teammate themselves, using the same Forgot Your Password? link on the login screen as if it were their own lockout.
Any user at all, from their own personal Settings page, since Settings can reset any account's password.
Only Salesforce Support can reset another user's password — no admin inside the org has that ability.
questions.explain: Resetting your own password is self-service, via Forgot Your Password? on the login screen. Resetting a teammate's password is a different, admin-side flow through Setup → Users → Reset Password(s), which requires admin permissions an ordinary user's personal Settings don't grant.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Setup page that shows an org's Organization ID, edition, instance, and license/storage usage all in one place is called ________.
questions.explain: Company Information is often the first page an experienced admin checks when opening an unfamiliar org — it summarizes identity (Organization ID), edition/instance, and the User Licenses and Data Storage tables, all on one page.

questions.prompt: An admin wants to create a new user, but the User Licenses table on Company Information shows Remaining Licenses at zero for the license type needed. What does this mean, per this course?
options: A license needs to be freed up or purchased before the new user can be created with that license type.
The org has hit its total Data Storage limit and needs to delete records before adding users.
The license count will automatically increase the next time someone logs in.
Remaining Licenses at zero only affects Chatter Free users, never a Salesforce license.
questions.explain: The User Licenses table's Total/Used/Remaining columns are exactly what to check before creating a new user. Remaining Licenses at zero for a given type means one must be freed up (for example, deactivating an unused user) or purchased before a new user of that type can be created.

questions.prompt: There's no literal 'reset' button for a Salesforce org. Put these steps, per this course, in the order that gets the practical equivalent of a clean-slate org.
items: Go to the Hands-On Orgs page
Disconnect the playground you want to leave behind
Click Create Playground to provision a genuinely fresh org
Confirm the new org comes back with only the default sample data
questions.explain: Since there's no one-click reset, the real equivalent is: go to Hands-On Orgs, disconnect the old playground (removing it from your list without deleting the org itself), create a brand-new playground, and confirm it comes back empty except for the default sample records.

questions.prompt: A brand-new Trailhead Playground opens for the first time. Per this course, what should you expect to already see?
options: A small set of pre-loaded sample records, like an Account named 'Acme' and an Opportunity marked '(Sample)'.
A completely empty org with zero records of any kind until you import your own data.
A fully built-out 'Coral Cloud Resorts' sample app installed automatically on every new org.
A locked Setup menu until you complete your first Trailhead module.
questions.explain: A freshly created org isn't a blank slate — Salesforce pre-loads a small set of sample records, like Acme accounts and opportunities clearly marked '(Sample)' in the record name, so there's something real to click into immediately. Full sample apps like Coral Cloud Resorts have to be installed separately from the Sample Gallery, not by default.

questions.prompt: Per this course, why does it recommend reusing one Trailhead Playground across every course in a career path, instead of creating a new one per course?
options: Fragmenting work across several playgrounds costs more in confusion — remembering which org has which setup — than one, slightly busier org ever will.
Trailhead only allows one playground to exist per Trailblazer account at any time.
A new playground created after the first one inherits none of Setup's admin features.
Only the very first playground you create is eligible to earn Trailhead badges.
questions.explain: The course's reasoning is practical, not a platform limit: switching between several different playgrounds and trying to remember which has which setup costs more than keeping one, progressively busier org that you commit to and log into periodically.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: renaming a Trailhead Playground on the Hands-On Orgs page only changes its display label — it has no effect on the org's actual login ________.
questions.explain: Rename only updates the label shown on the Hands-On Orgs page; it's completely safe to do at any time because it never touches the org's real login username.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about organizing a permanent training org, per this course.
options: Prefixing test records or custom objects by course makes it obvious later which course a piece of work came from.
Dating test data, like 'Test Account 2026-10,' is more useful months later than a generic name like 'Test Account 3.'
Salesforce's built-in Notes object can attach context to a record without leaving the org.
Clean, consistent naming only matters for records you create by hand, never for data brought in through the Data Import Wizard.
A permanent training org should never have any records deleted from it, ever, under any circumstance.
questions.explain: Course-prefixed names, dated test data, and the built-in Notes object are the three real habits this lesson recommends. Naming discipline matters for imported data too — the Data Import Wizard's field-mapping step only goes smoothly with clear source column names — and periodic cleanup, including deleting records you're done with, is explicitly encouraged, not forbidden.

questions.prompt: A learner finishes a Trailhead module's hands-on challenge and clicks 'Check Challenge.' Per this course, what actually makes that challenge pass or fail?
options: Trailhead verifies the actual state of the learner's connected org — did the field, flow, or object really get created — not just that they clicked a button claiming completion.
Trailhead only checks whether the learner spent a minimum number of minutes on the page before clicking Check Challenge.
Trailhead asks the learner a multiple-choice question about the lesson's content instead of inspecting their org.
Trailhead automatically passes every challenge the first time it's attempted, regardless of the org's state.
questions.explain: Trailhead's verification checks the learner's actual connected org to confirm the hands-on work was genuinely done, which is exactly what makes a Trailblazer profile's badges a checkable credential rather than a self-reported list.

questions.prompt: Per this course's recommended troubleshooting order, where should an admin look first when stuck on a 'how do I configure X' question, before turning to Trailhead modules or the Trailblazer Community?
options: help.salesforce.com, the official documentation site.
The Trailblazer Community, since real admins respond faster than documentation can be searched.
LTV's own course labs, since they're built specifically to answer Salesforce Setup questions.
The App Launcher's search box, since it searches Salesforce's documentation directly.
questions.explain: This course's troubleshooting order is: help.salesforce.com first as the most reliable stop for a 'how do I' question, then Trailhead's own modules for more depth, then the Trailblazer Community for real admins who've likely hit the exact same problem.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 3 Trailhead concept to what it actually is.
right: Your public, verified record of completed badges, points, and trails
A step-by-step Trailhead learning unit with an auto-verified hands-on challenge
Salesforce's public Q&A and networking community for admins and developers
questions.explain: A Module is a step-by-step learning unit with an auto-verified hands-on challenge. A Superbadge is instruction-free and scenario-based. The Trailblazer Community is Salesforce's public Q&A and networking space. A Trailblazer profile is the public, verified record of your completed badges, points, and trails.
